# Our Models

Ensembles of simpler forecasters

## Our Models: Baselines

::: {.notes}
Our typical forecast submission is an ensemble of several models.
These assume the data is untrustworthy in some way. (linear throws out old data, climate_base throws out historical data).

Contrast with the current baseline which just forecasts today's value forwards.
:::

- `linear`: linearly extrapolate the last 4 weeks, quantiles from the fit error
- `climate_base`: a climatological model, quantiles estimated from a 7 week period centered on the `target_date`'s season week from historical data for that geo

- `climate_linear`: a weighted ensemble of the climatological and linear, depending on the ahead and quantile

## Our Models: Baselines

```{r demo_climate_linear, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 16, echo=FALSE}
plot_geos <- c("pa", "mi")
demo_start <- as.Date("2024-11-15")
demo_date <- as.Date("2025-02-19")
demo_end <- as.Date("2025-04-15")
filtered_flu_forecasts <-
  flu_forecasts %>%
  filter(quantile %in% c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.75, 0.9, 0.95), geo_value %in% plot_geos) %>%
  filter(forecaster %in% c("climate_base", "linear", "climate_linear"))

flu_forecast_plt <-
  filtered_flu_forecasts %>%
  filter(forecast_date == demo_date) %>%
  mutate(forecaster = factor(forecaster, levels = c("linear", "climate_base", "climate_linear"))) %>%
  left_join(state_census, by = join_by(geo_value == abbr)) %>%
  mutate(value = value * 1e5 / pop) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = quantile, values_from = value) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = target_end_date)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = `0.05`, ymax = `0.95`, color = NA, fill = forecaster, group = forecast_date), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = `0.1`, ymax = `0.9`, color = NA, fill = forecaster, group = forecast_date), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = `0.25`, ymax = `0.75`, color = NA, fill = forecaster, group = forecast_date), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = `0.4`, ymax = `0.6`, color = NA, fill = forecaster, group = forecast_date), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = `0.5`, color = forecaster, group = forecast_date), size = 1.2) +
  geom_line(
    data = flu_current %>%
      filter(time_value > demo_start, time_value < demo_end, geo_value %in% plot_geos) %>%
      left_join(state_census, by = join_by(geo_value == abbr)) %>%
      mutate(value = value * 1e5 / pop),
    aes(x = time_value, y = value)) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  facet_grid(geo_value ~ forecaster, scale = "free") +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  scale_x_date(breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 16)) +
  ylab("rates")

flu_forecast_plt
```

:::{.notes}
`climate_linear` is ~linear at the start, and ~ climate at the end.
Chosen to clearly represent behavior, atypically good.
:::

## Our Models: Autoregressive

`windowed_seasonal`: an AR model trained on data from the same seasonal window in previous years

$$x_{t+h} = a_0 + a_1 \cdot x_{t-7} + a_2 \cdot x_{t-14}$$

- $x$ is hospitalization rates, $t$ is the forecast date, $h$ is the horizon in days
- built using [epipredict](https://cmu-delphi.github.io/epipredict/)
- training data: 3 weeks before now through 5 weeks after the target date (-3/+8 from now)

```{r windowed_seasonal_illustration, fig.width=25, fig.height=3.2, echo=FALSE, out.extra='class="r-stretch"'}
demo_week <- 10
backward_window <- 3
forward_window <- 5
max_ahead <- 3
anomalous <- c("2020/21", "2021/22")
seasons <- c("2020/21", "2021/22", "2022/23", "2023/24", "2024/25", "2025/26")
week_min <- -5
week_max <- 26

pal <- RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(8, "Set2")
target_week <- demo_week + max_ahead
window_left  <- demo_week - backward_window
window_right <- target_week + forward_window

x_breaks <- c(seq(week_min + 1, 0, by = 2), seq(1, week_max, by = 5))
x_labels <- ifelse(x_breaks <= 0, as.character(52 + x_breaks), as.character(x_breaks))

tidyr::expand_grid(
  season = factor(seasons, levels = rev(seasons)),
  season_week = week_min:week_max
) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(category = dplyr::case_when(
    season %in% anomalous                                          ~ "excluded (anomalous)",
    season == "2025/26" & season_week == demo_week                                    ~ "forecast date",
    season == "2025/26" & season_week == target_week                                  ~ "target date",
    season == "2025/26" & season_week > demo_week                                     ~ "unobserved",
    season == "2025/26" & ((season_week == demo_week - 1) | (season_week == demo_week - 2))                                ~ "predictor",
    season == "2025/26" & season_week >= window_left & season_week <= demo_week - 2   ~ "training window",
    season == "2025/26" & ((season_week == window_left - 1) | (season_week == window_left - 2))                              ~ "predictor",
    season == "2025/26"                                                               ~ "observed and discarded",
    season_week >= window_left & season_week <= window_right       ~ "training window",
    !(season %in% anomalous) & ((season_week == window_left - 1) | (season_week == window_left - 2)) ~ "predictor",
    TRUE                                                       ~ "observed and discarded"
  )) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = season_week, y = season, fill = category)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = window_left - 0.5,
             linetype = "dashed", color = "#2ca25f", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = window_right + 0.5,
             linetype = "dashed", color = "#2ca25f", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = demo_week,
             linetype = "solid", color = pal[2], linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted", color = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = -2.5,      y = 6.7,  label = "← prior yr", size = 7,   color = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = demo_week,   y = -0.15, label = "now",   size = 6.5, color = pal[2], vjust = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = target_week, y = -0.15, label = "+3 wk", size = 6.5, color = pal[4], vjust = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "",
    values = c(
      "training window"       = pal[1],
      "forecast date"         = pal[2],
      "target date"           = pal[4],
      "predictor"             = pal[3],
      "observed and discarded" = "#d9d9d9",
      "unobserved"            = "#f0f0f0",
      "excluded (anomalous)"  = "#bdbdbd"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = x_breaks, labels = x_labels, name = "Week") +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(y = "") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right",
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_blank(),
    axis.line = element_line(colour = "grey50"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 16),
    legend.key.size = unit(0.7, "cm"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 17),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 5, r = 5, b = 30, l = 5)
  )
```

::: {.notes}
The "training window" approach to handling seasonality gave a large improvement over a plain AR model.
:::

## Our Models: Autoregressive
For forecasting NSSP for either flu or covid, since it is a rate to begin with, we just use that 2 term autoregressive model, using all states as training data.

## Our Models: Autoregressive — Data Preprocessing

NHSN reports **counts**; we convert to **rates per 100k** before forecasting

For Flu, we also augment with ILI+ and FluSURV data (inspired by Flusion), then whiten on a per-geo+source basis:

- NHSN usable data: **2 seasons** (2022/23–2023/24, excluding pandemic years)
- ILI+ extends this to **~25 seasons** (back to 1997)
- FluSURV extends this another **~11 seasons** (back to 2009/10)

To make these comparable, we normalize in several ways:


1. **Variance stabilization** — 4th root transform
2. **Scaling** — divide by the inter-quantile range (5th–95th percentile)
3. **Centering** — subtract so that the median is zero

::: {.notes}
The augmented data sources improved the model score.
We did not see much improvement from adding more lags or tweaking the whitening settings.
Covid uses rates directly across all states; no whitening.
:::

## Our Models: Autoregressive with Exogenous Predictors

`windowed_seasonal_nssp`: adds NSSP emergency department visits as an exogenous predictor

$$x_{t+h} = a_0 + a_1 x_{t-7} + a_2 x_{t-14} + a_3 y_{t-7} + a_4 y_{t-14}$$

- $y$ is NSSP (ED visit rates) — a leading indicator for hospitalizations
- no whitening, no augmented sources (NSSP doesn't go back far enough)
- same formulation for both Flu and Covid

::: {.notes}
Also tried Google Symptoms and NWSS state-level aggregations — no meaningful improvement.
ED visits lead hospitalizations by ~1 week, so the signal is real but modest.
:::

## Our Models: Autoregressive — Fitting

We use **quantile regression** via [epipredict](https://cmu-delphi.github.io/epipredict/reference/quantile_reg.html), which wraps the standard [quantreg](https://rdrr.io/cran/quantreg/) package:

- Each quantile level $\tau$ is fit as a **separate weighted linear program**:

$$\minimize_{\beta} \sum_i w_i \cdot L(y_i,\, x_i^\top \beta)$$

- The **pinball loss** penalises under- and over-shoots asymmetrically:

$$L(y, t) := \begin{cases} (1-\tau)(t - y), & y < t \\ \tau(y - t), & y \geq t \end{cases}$$

::: {.notes}
This is the standard quantile regression / pinball loss / check function setup.
The weighted LP formulation means no closed-form solution, but it's fast enough in practice.
Directly optimises the WIS scoring metric used for evaluation.
:::

## Our Models: Ensemble

Our submission (`CMU-TimeSeries`) is a **weighted ensemble** of the component models, with geo-level weights

- Weights are (nominally) set manually each week based on performance and data quality
- **2024/25**: initially relied heavily on `climate_linear` — the season started late and we were unsure of data quality. Eventually transitioned back to AR forecasters
- **2025/26**: almost exclusively `windowed_seasonal_nssp` (NSSP exogenous), with a small contribution from `windowed_seasonal` (the whitening AR) for Flu

::: {.notes}
The geo-level weights let us down-weight or exclude forecasters for specific states where data quality is poor or a model is known to misbehave.
The shift from climate_linear to nssp reflects the NSSP data becoming more reliable and the season being more "normal".
:::

## Infrastructure

**Pipeline**: weekly automated runs via [`targets`](https://docs.ropensci.org/targets/) + [`epipredict`](https://cmu-delphi.github.io/epipredict/)

- Each model variant is a target; `targets` skips recomputation when inputs haven't changed
- Forecasts and scores uploaded to S3; rendered notebooks for review each week
- Use of make to handle shared environmental variables, submitting after manual checks and any adjustments


::: {.notes}
The targets pipeline means the whole run is reproducible and incremental — adding a new forecast date only reruns the affected targets.
The exploration grid was run as a backtest over 2023/24 and 2024/25; the best-performing configs (by WIS) informed the production ensemble choices.
We ended up with windowed_seasonal_nssp as the clear winner once NSSP data quality stabilised.
:::

## Model Selection
**Exploration**: backtest over the 2023/24 season of versioned data with several model variants

- lags, up to 5 weeks back
- Exogenous sources: NSSP, NWSS, NWSS region, Veteran's affairs, google symptoms
- Seasonal augmentation methods: 
  + windowed (various sizes, {3, 5, 7} weeks × forward ∈ {1, 3, 5} weeks)
  + Aux signals:
    - seasonal sinusoid
    - PCA
    - climatological
- Residual whitening: on/off
